title: Tooth surfaces & cavity classification
blurb: Mesial, distal, occlusal, incisal, buccal, labial, lingual and palatal, plus Black's cavity classes I to V.
question: The dentist is charting and says: 'Two-six, MOD amalgam. One-one, distal cavity involving the incisal corner. Lower incisors, calculus on the inner surfaces.' Which surfaces are these, and which of Black's classes is the cavity on 11?

teach.body: Every tooth has five surfaces, and naming them lets the team chart exactly where decay, a filling or a deposit is. Two face the neighbouring teeth: mesial and distal. One faces outwards towards the cheeks or lips: buccal or labial. One faces inwards towards the tongue or palate: lingual or palatal. The last is the biting surface: the occlusal surface on premolars and molars, or the incisal edge on incisors and canines.

teach.h: The surfaces on a charting diagram
teach.caption: Each square is a tooth seen from above, opened out flat. The centre is the biting surface; the four sides are the walls. Mesial always points towards the midline.

teach.h: Mesial, distal and the spaces between
teach.body: Mesial and distal follow the curve of the arch, not left and right. The mesial surface is the one nearer the midline; the distal is further away. So where two teeth touch, the distal of one meets the mesial of the next, except between the two central incisors, where mesial meets mesial. Together, mesial and distal surfaces are the proximal (interproximal) surfaces. The area near the gum, where crown meets root, is called cervical.

Some surfaces are far more at risk. Occlusal pits and fissures trap plaque and food, which is why they are fissure sealed. Proximal surfaces below the contact point can't be reached by a brush, so they need interdental cleaning. Cervical margins collect plaque at the gum line. Lingual surfaces of the lower incisors are often missed and build up calculus, so if a patient misses them, advise improving brushing there. Grinding wears flat shiny facets on occlusal and incisal surfaces.

teach.caption: The molar on the right shows its occlusal surface: raised cusps separated by deep fissures and pits. These grooves are the most plaque- and caries-prone part of a posterior tooth.

teach.body: A cavity or filling often covers more than one surface, so the abbreviations are joined: MO (mesio-occlusal), DO (disto-occlusal) or MOD (mesial, occlusal and distal). More than a century ago, the American dentist G.V. Black grouped cavities by where they start, and dentists still use his classes when planning and recording restorations. Knowing them helps you anticipate the materials and matrix the dentist will want: a Class II, for example, usually needs a matrix band to rebuild the missing proximal wall.

teach.caption: Some texts add Class VI: cusp tips and incisal edges.

teach.text: Match the word to the tooth. Buccal = cheek side of BACK teeth; labial = lip side of FRONT teeth. Palatal = inner side of UPPER teeth; lingual = inner side of LOWER teeth (some questions use 'lingual' for any inner surface, so pick it if palatal isn't offered). Class III and IV are both proximal on front teeth: IV is the one that takes in the incisal angle.

items: Mesial = towards the midline; distal = away; together they are the proximal surfaces.
Occlusal = chewing surface of premolars and molars; incisal = biting edge of incisors and canines.
Buccal (cheek, posterior), labial (lips, anterior), palatal (upper inner), lingual (lower inner).
Pits, fissures and proximal surfaces are the most caries-prone.
Black: I pits/fissures, II posterior proximal, III anterior proximal, IV anterior proximal + incisal angle, V cervical.

summary: You can now name and locate every tooth surface, use the correct term for anterior and posterior, upper and lower teeth, read combined surface codes such as MOD, explain which surfaces are most at risk of plaque and decay, and classify cavities using Black's Classes I to V.

A.q: A patient has plaque building up mainly on the inner surfaces of their lower incisors, facing the tongue. Which surface is most affected?
A.why: The surface of a lower tooth facing the tongue is the lingual surface.

whyNot.0: The labial surface faces the lips, on the outside.
whyNot.2: The distal surface faces away from the midline, towards the next tooth.
whyNot.3: Palatal is used for the inner surface of UPPER teeth, facing the palate.

A.q: The dentist diagnoses a cavity between two lower molars, starting on the proximal surface. Which of Black's classes is this?
A.why: Class II cavities start on the proximal (mesial or distal) surfaces of premolars and molars.

whyNot.0: Class I cavities start in pits and fissures.
whyNot.1: Class III is proximal on incisors and canines, not molars.
whyNot.3: Class V cavities are in the cervical third, near the gum line.

A.q: You are charting cavities. Which description matches the mesial surface?
options: The surface furthest from the midline
The surface closest to the midline
A.why: Mesial means the surface nearest the midline, following the curve of the arch.

whyNot.0: The surface facing the cheek is buccal.
whyNot.1: The surface furthest from the midline is distal.
whyNot.2: The surface facing the tongue is lingual.

B.q: The dentist asks you to focus the polishing cup on the surfaces of the upper molars that face the cheeks. Which surfaces are these?
B.why: The cheek-facing surfaces of premolars and molars are buccal.

whyNot.0: Palatal surfaces face the palate, on the inside of the upper teeth.
whyNot.1: Labial is for the lip-facing surfaces of front teeth.
whyNot.3: Distal surfaces face away from the midline, towards the back.

B.q: A patient chips the biting edge of an upper incisor on a glass bottle. Which surface is involved?
B.why: The biting edge of an incisor or canine is the incisal edge.

whyNot.0: Occlusal describes the chewing surface of premolars and molars.
whyNot.2: The labial surface is the front face, not the biting edge.
whyNot.3: The cervical margin is at the neck of the tooth, near the gum.

B.q: A cavity has formed at the gum line on the labial surface of a lower canine. How is it classified?
B.why: Class V cavities are in the cervical third of the labial/buccal or lingual/palatal surface of any tooth.

whyNot.1: Class III starts on a proximal surface of an anterior tooth.
whyNot.2: Class IV is proximal on an anterior tooth and involves the incisal angle.
whyNot.3: Class I starts in pits and fissures.

C.q: Which surface of an upper central incisor faces the roof of the mouth?
C.why: The inner surface of an upper tooth faces the palate, so it is the palatal surface.

whyNot.0: The labial surface faces the lips.
whyNot.1: Buccal describes the cheek-facing surface of back teeth.
whyNot.2: The incisal edge is the biting edge.

C.q: The dentist tells a patient to clean between their teeth with interdental brushes to prevent decay. Which surfaces does this target?
C.why: Interdental cleaning reaches the proximal surfaces: mesial and distal.

whyNot.0: Buccal and lingual surfaces can be reached with a toothbrush.
whyNot.2: Occlusal and incisal are biting surfaces, cleaned by brushing.
whyNot.3: Labial and palatal surfaces face outwards and inwards, not between teeth.

C.q: A cavity on the mesial surface of 21 has spread to include the incisal corner. Which of Black's classes is it?
C.why: A proximal cavity on an anterior tooth that involves the incisal angle is Class IV.

whyNot.0: Class II is proximal on premolars and molars, not incisors.
whyNot.1: Class III is proximal on an anterior tooth with the incisal angle still intact.
whyNot.3: Class V is a cervical (gum-line) cavity.

reteach.title: A tooth is a house in a terrace
reteach.question: Picture each tooth as a house in a curved terrace, with the town centre at the midline. Which wall is which?

blocks.body: The side wall facing the town centre is mesial; the side wall facing out of town is distal. Next-door houses share walls, which is why proximal surfaces are hard to clean. The front door opens onto the street: that's the cheeks (buccal) for back teeth or the lips (labial) for front teeth. The back garden faces the palate (palatal) upstairs or the tongue (lingual) downstairs. The roof is where the work happens: a flat-ish occlusal surface or a sharp incisal edge.

explain.body: Premolars and molars chew with an occlusal surface of cusps, pits and fissures. Incisors and canines bite with an incisal edge. Grinding leaves flat, shiny wear facets on these surfaces.

test.q: The dentist notes wear facets on the chewing surfaces of a patient's molars. Which surfaces are these?
test.why: The chewing surfaces of premolars and molars are the occlusal surfaces.

whyNot.0: Incisal describes the biting edge of front teeth.
whyNot.3: Cervical describes the neck of the tooth near the gum.

explain.body: Mesial faces the midline along the arch; distal faces away. The distal of one tooth touches the mesial of the next. Together they are the proximal surfaces, cleaned interdentally.

explain.caption: The distal surface of 34 touches the mesial surface of 35.

test.q: A filling is on the surface of tooth 34 that touches tooth 35. Which surface is it?
test.why: 35 is further from the midline than 34, so the surface of 34 that touches it is the distal surface.

whyNot.0: The mesial surface of 34 faces the canine (33), towards the midline.
whyNot.2: Buccal faces the cheek, not a neighbouring tooth.
whyNot.3: Lingual faces the tongue, not a neighbouring tooth.

explain.body: Outer: buccal for back teeth (cheek), labial for front teeth (lips). Inner: palatal for upper teeth, lingual for lower teeth.

test.q: Which term describes the surface of tooth 13 that faces the lips?
test.why: 13 is an anterior tooth (upper right canine), so the lip-facing surface is labial.

whyNot.0: Buccal is used for the cheek-facing surface of back teeth.
whyNot.1: Palatal is the inner surface of an upper tooth.
whyNot.2: Lingual is the inner surface of a lower tooth.

explain.body: I: pits and fissures. II: proximal, posterior teeth. III: proximal, anterior teeth, incisal angle intact. IV: proximal, anterior teeth, incisal angle involved. V: cervical third of any tooth.

test.q: Where do Black's Class I cavities start?
test.why: Class I cavities start in pits and fissures, such as the occlusal surfaces of molars.

whyNot.1: Proximal surfaces of posterior teeth are Class II.
whyNot.3: Involvement of the incisal angle makes a Class IV.
